title: Awareness was never the problem
lede: Coors backed Zima with one of the largest launch budgets in its history and a campaign that deliberately refused to explain the product. It bought a year of curiosity.

blocks.title: The pitchman
blocks.body:
Foote, Cone & Belding’s San Francisco office made the campaign. It cast the comedian Roger Kabler as a stranger in a black hat who turned up in bars, swapped his S’s for Z’s and recommended “zomething different.”[^12][^13] The agency’s Scott Rabschnuck told Westword in 1995 that they had wanted “someone fun and kind of funny and a little bit quirky,” and admitted to overdoing it: the character “went from different and unique to being eccentric and weird.”[^12]

Letterman’s jokes were at first treated as free publicity. Rabschnuck said some people on the public relations side “encouraged Letterman by sending him cases of Zima.”[^12]

In 1995 the hat was retired. The replacement campaign, “zomething in common,” showed young men and women playing touch football and eating in a diner, in black and white, with no dialogue.[^12]

blocks.title: An early brand website
blocks.body: Zima also had a telephone hotline printed on the bottle, an e-mail address and, by 1995, a site at zima.com. Its FAQ credits Modem Media of Westport, Connecticut, with “all the interactive initiatives via computer-based media.”[^33] Westword described the site in 1995 as a serial about a character named Duncan, and in 2005 called it “highly ambitious” next to the single page that then stood at zimaxxx.com.[^12][^22] Screenshots of the 1996 site are in the website section below.
